extracted.intended_audience: plant breeders, seed/plant companies, agricultural innovators, and their counsel seeking U.S. IP protection for new plant varieties
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the available forms of intellectual property protection in the United States for new plant varieties (plant patents, utility patents, and Plant Variety Protection certificates), their eligibility requirements, scope of rights, procedural differences, and strategic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant patent eligibility (new, distinct, asexually reproduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant patent protects a new, distinct, and asexually reproduced plant variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To meet the “new” requirement the plant must be a new variety not known or used by others before the plant patent application is filed. Distinctiveness can be based on characteristics such as flower color, leaf shape, flavor, growth habit, method and ease of reproduction, or other unique traits. Asexually propagated plants are those reproduced by means other than from fertilized seeds; any asexual reproduction method that provides a genetic copy can be used. Note exclusions: tuber propagated plants (e.g., potatoes) or plants found in an uncultivated state are not eligible for plant patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant patent claim and scope (one claim / one plant/genome; rights under 35 U.S.C. § 163)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant patent has only one claim and protects one plant or genome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plant patent holder has exclusive rights to prevent others from asexually reproducing the plant, and from using, offering for sale, or selling the patented plant or its parts, or from importing the patented plant, or any parts thereof. (35 U.S.C. § 163).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility patent eligibility and scope for plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility patents can protect plants that are asexually reproduced, sexually reproduced, or tuber propagated and may protect groups of plants, plant parts, non-naturally occurring substances isolated from plants, and breeding methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility patents are typically used for transgenic plants where genetic material is altered to confer benefits (drought resistance, pest resistance, higher yield). Utility patent coverage is broader than plant patents or PVP certificates but is generally more difficult to obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility patent enablement/written description via biological deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant can optionally submit biological deposits (e.g., seeds or propagation materials) at an internationally recognized deposition facility; deposits are treated as part of the application disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such deposits can help satisfy the written description, particularly the enablement requirement, by providing material support for the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner of a utility patent can exclude others from making, using, selling, offering to sell, or importing the patented invention into the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard statutory exclusionary scope for utility patents and applies to plant-related utility patents as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVP certificate eligibility (new, distinct, uniform, stable)
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify for a Plant Variety Protection (PVP) certificate, applicants must show their variety is new, distinct, uniform, and stable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformness can be demonstrated if variations are describable, predictable, and commercially acceptable. Stability can be shown if the plant variety is not changed from one generation to the next. PVPs are administered by USDA under the PVPA (U.S. implementation of UPOV). PVP certificates apply to sexually reproduced, asexually reproduced, or tuber-propagated varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVP deposit requirements (sexually/tuber vs asexually reproduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposit is not required for asexually reproduced varieties; a seed or plant tissue deposit is required for sexually or tuber propagated varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits serve as the accessible material for examination/verification for PVP applications when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVP grace periods (domestic, foreign-only, tree/vine)
rubrics_metrics.description: PVP certificates allow a one-year grace period for seed sold or offered for sale in the U.S., a four-year grace period if the variety has only been sold in a foreign country, and a six-year grace period for a tree or vine sold anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with plant and utility patents which may have a one-year grace period under certain circumstances; the longer PVP grace periods can make PVP preferable in some commercial situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVP exclusivity / prohibited acts by others
rubrics_metrics.description: The owner of a PVP certificate can exclude others from selling, marketing, offering to buy or sell, delivering, consigning, exchanging, importing or exporting the variety, sexually multiplying or propagating the variety by tuber, using the variety in producing a hybrid, or conditioning the variety for the purpose of propagation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerates the commercial acts that the PVP owner can prohibit, defining the scope of PVP protection in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVP statutory exemptions (research and right to save seed)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two exemptions to PVP exclusivity: a research exemption and a right to save seed exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The research exemption allows use of the certified variety for breeding to develop a new variety. Under the right to save seed exemption, one can save a seed that was lawfully obtained from the breeder for the sole use of replanting on one’s land (i.e., limited farmer-saved seed privilege).

rubrics_metrics.name: Term length differences (PVP vs patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: PVP certificates generally provide 25 years for trees and vines and 20 years for other varieties from the date the certificate is issued; plant and utility patents have a 20-year term from the effective application filing date, subject to patent term adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PVP certificate terms are counted from issue date and can be longer than patent terms in some cases; this timing difference affects strategic choice of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility/ineligibility interplay among protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all plants can qualify for all three forms of IP protection; e.g., sexually reproduced or tuber propagated varieties are not eligible for plant patent protection but may be protected by a utility patent or a PVP certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plant variety may be barred from a plant or utility patent application but otherwise qualify for a PVP certificate due to PVP's longer grace periods under certain circumstances. Conversely, utility patents can cover things PVP or plant patents cannot (e.g., non-naturally occurring substances, breeding methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic choice and stacking of protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing which form(s) of plant IP protection to pursue depends on the specific innovation, the innovator’s business needs, and other factors; multiple forms of protection are not mutually exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility patents often offer broader scope but are harder to obtain; plant patents and PVP certificates can be easier or offer other advantages (e.g., grace periods). Obtaining multiple protections can deter infringers by increasing litigation/licensing costs.
